links.outcome: Change in obesity risk attribution when child demographic attributes varied in prompts
links.effect: Socioeconomic status produced low-income attribution in 40/42 decisions (decision change rate 19.0%); urban-rural decision change rate 52.4%; most models attributed higher risk to Black and Hispanic/Latino children.
links.quote: Socioeconomic status produced the most consistent attribution pattern (low-income attribution in 40/42 decisions; decision change rate 19.0%).

links.outcome: Neutral-prompt scores for stigmatizing language, representation and cultural fit across seven LLMs
links.effect: All models had a 100% Stigmatizing/Harmful Language pass rate, but representation and cultural fit were universally weak; Claude mean 3.00 ± 0.91 vs GLM 1.44 ± 0.51.
links.quote: All models achieved a 100% Stigmatizing/Harmful Language pass rate, yet representation and cultural fit were universally weak.

links.outcome: Differences in LLM obesity risk attribution across demographic subgroups and between models
links.effect: Between-model differences significant (Kruskal-Wallis H = 46.21, p < 0.001); urban-rural attribution directionally inconsistent across models, with Western models favoring rural and Chinese-origin models urban attribution.
links.quote: Urban-rural attribution showed the greatest cross-model directional inconsistency (decision change rate 52.4%), with Western-origin models favoring rural attribution and Chinese-origin models favoring urban attribution.

screen.reason: Empirical evaluation of demographic bias across seven LLMs in pediatric obesity risk attribution using prompt-based benchmark testing.
